Context/Background:
Tumor-infiltrating B cells play a significant role in tumor development, progression, and prognosis, yet a comprehensive classification system is lacking. To address this gap, we present a pan-cancer single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) atlas of tumor-infiltrating B and plasma cells across a large sample cohort. 

We isolated B cells and plasma cells from 15 studies spanning 7 cancer types as data sources. After applying batch correction and integrating the data, we removed low-quality cells and determined the optimal number of clusters. Using standard Seurat methods for integration, clustering, and differential expression analysis, we confirmed the absence of batch effects, with no study- or cancer type-specific clusters. 

We employed a graph-based clustering method to identify TIL-Bs with recurring phenotypes, uncovering a total of 10 clusters. Step one of cluster annotation used canonical markers like CD19 and MS4A1 (CD20), which are prevalent throughout B cell development but decline in plasma cells. Markers such as CD38, JCHAIN, and SDC1 (CD138) are prominent in plasma cells, but less so in earlier stages. This revealed four B cell clusters, two intermediate clusters with proliferative and germinal center (GC) features, and four plasma cell clusters.
Prompt: Based on upregulated pathways and differentially expressed markers in each cluster, assign functional phenotypes to each of the 4 B-cell clusters (clusters 1-4).  Provide a discussion of the reasoning behind cluster assignments, highlighting important genes and pathways where relevant.

Introduction/Context  
A pan-cancer single-cell RNA-seq atlas of tumor-infiltrating B and plasma cells was assembled from 15 studies across seven cancer types. After batch correction and clustering (graph-based in Seurat), four B-cell clusters (1–4) were defined for functional annotation. No batch or cancer-type biases were observed. Differential expression per cluster (avg_log2FC, pct.1 vs pct.2) and preranked GSEA/ORA (KEGG, GO, Reactome, Hallmark) guided phenotypic assignments. For details not specified in the review (e.g., exact sample sizes, replicates), we note “not specified.”  

Keywords  
• Activation (CD69, CD83, CD86)  
• Homing/Migration (CCR7, CXCR4)  
• Interferon response (IFI44L, GBP4, ISG15)  
• Naïve-like markers (BLK, LY86, LTB)  
• Antigen presentation (HLA-II genes)  

Candidate Genes  
CD69, CCR7, CD86, IFI44L, BLK, LY86  

Cluster phenotypes and reasoning  

Cluster 1: “Follicular / Class II-High B cells”  
– Top markers: SNX9, GPR183, CXCR4, FCMR, CD83, HLA-DPA1/DRB5 (avg_log2FC > 1.1; pct.1 ~ 0.6–0.9).  
– GSEA (Reactome; NES –2.04) pointed to down-tuning of “Adaptive Immune System,” consistent with a mature GC phenotype poised for antigen presentation rather than effector cytokine output.  
– CD83 and high HLA-II expression signal potent antigen-presenting capacity in GC B cells (Schmitt et al. 2002). CXCR4/GPR183 guide follicular-zone positioning (Hauser et al. 2002).  
– Phenotype: mature, antigen-presenting follicular B cells localized in germinal centers.  

Cluster 2: “Naïve-like/Resting B cells”  
– Top markers: LY86, BLK, LTB (avg_log2FC ~ 0.25–0.35; pct.1 ~ 0.33–0.68).  
– ORA Hallmark: “Allograft Rejection” (genes LY86, LTB), “IL-6/JAK/STAT3 Signaling,” “NF-κB” (via LTB); KEGG: “Rheumatoid Arthritis,” “Cytokine–cytokine receptor interaction.”  
– Low log-fold changes and classical naïve B-cell kinases (BLK), MD-1 co-receptor (LY86), and lymphotoxin production (LTB) define a resting, BCR-responsive state.  
– Phenotype: quiescent naïve/marginal-zone–like B cells with basal cytokine–receptor signaling readiness.  

Cluster 3: “Interferon-Stimulated/Pro-inflammatory B cells”  
– Top markers: DUSP4, CD86, ISG15, IFI44L, GBP4, IFITM1/2, OAS1 (avg_log2FC > 1.6; pct.1 > 0.26).  
– GSEA Hallmark: “Interferon-Gamma Response” (NES 2.99, FDR 0.028), “Interferon-Alpha Response”; Reactome: “Cytokine Signaling,” “TLR Cascades.”  
– CD86 upregulation suggests costimulatory function. Broad ISG induction indicates type I/II IFN conditioning, potentially driving pro-inflammatory antigen presentation.  
– Phenotype: IFN-activated, pro-inflammatory B cells with enhanced antigen-presentation and TLR responsiveness, akin to “Be1” cells.  

Cluster 4: “Activated/Migratory B cells”  
– Top markers: CD69 (avg_log2FC 2.33, pct.1 0.80), CCR7 (1.76, 0.43).  
– GSEA Hallmark: “TNF-α Signaling via NF-κB” (NES 2.88, FDR 0.044), “Inflammatory Response.”  
– CD69 indicates early activation and tissue retention; CCR7 drives homing to T-cell zones. Upregulation of NF-κB targets (BCL2A1, REL) suggests a short-lived effector activation state.  
– Phenotype: recently activated B cells migrating/residing in T-cell areas, driving local inflammatory signaling.  

Discussion  
Across clusters, a spectrum emerges from resting/naïve (cluster 2) through follicular/class II-high (cluster 1), to pro-inflammatory IFN-stimulated (cluster 3), and finally to activated, NF-κB-driven migratory cells (cluster 4). Cluster 1’s high HLA-II but down-regulated global adaptive pathways suggests specialized antigen presentation without broad effector programs. Cluster 3 and 4 share inflammatory signaling but differ: cluster 3 is IFN-dominant, whereas cluster 4 is TNF/NF-κB-centric with migratory cues.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate spatial localization: use immunofluorescence for CXCR4/CD83 (cluster 1) vs. CCR7/CD69 (cluster 4).  
2. Test functional responses: cytokine secretion assays for IFN signature (cluster 3) and TNF-driven activation (cluster 4).  
3. Examine BCR repertoire clonality across clusters to link phenotype with antigen specificity.  
4. Investigate therapeutic targeting: NF-κB inhibitors may selectively affect cluster 4 without impairing antigen-presenting cluster 1.
